title: Synthetic traffic calibration — warmup drift mitigation and repeatability playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for calibrating synthetic traffic and taming warmup drift in our throughput harness. Goal is repeatable, explainable throughput numbers across runs and machines so that:
- PR-level performance regressions are actionable
- Papering over cache/priming noise is minimized
- We can compare kernel/runtime changes deterministically as much as possible

Context / problem we keep hitting:
Over the last quarter we saw run-to-run variance of 5–18% in aggregate tokens/sec on the same commit across identical GPU nodes. Root causes observed include:
- implicit KV/prefix cache state from prior requests
- sequence-length distribution mismatch between runs (long sequences change kernel selection and memory pressure)
- randomized sampling in synthetic prompt generator (seed drift)
- delayed memory allocation patterns in libdevice/cuBLAS causing early throughput oscillations
- thermal/BF16/quantization path differences depending on first few batches

High-level approach:
1) Reduce non-determinism surface (seed RNGs, pin batch shapes)
2) Measure and ensure a fixed priming phase that stabilizes caches/state
3) Use burn-in/measurement windows and cross-check with diagnostic traces (GPU metrics + tracing)
4) Capture and normalize any remaining drift statistically (median of N runs, run-level meta)

Experiment design details (recommended default config):
- Harness: local loadgen harness with worker processes pinned to cores; separate driver that orchestrates client/agent.
- Run length: 20 minute total per experiment (5m warmup / 12m steady measurement / 3m cooldown).
- Ramp policy: linear ramp to target QPS over 60s (avoid instant burst).
- Seed policy: fixed seed per run (default 42) and per-worker offset seeds (seed + worker_id).
- Prompt/seq length distribution: explicit config string (short:0.7, medium:0.25, long:0.05). Do not rely on uniform random if you want repeatability.
- Deterministic tokenization: use pre-tokenized prompt sets where possible, store token counts in run artifacts.

Sample loadgen CLI (conceptual):
python tools/loadgen.py \
  --target-qps 450 \
  --ramp-seconds 60 \
  --duration-seconds 1200 \
  --warmup-seconds 300 \
  --seed 42 \
  --seq-dist short:0.7,medium:0.25,long:0.05 \
  --prefill-prefixes data/priming-prefixes-v3.json \
  --record-trace /tmp/run-455.trace

Priming strategies (to remove first-request pathology):
- Explicit deterministic priming: before the measured window, send a fixed corpus of prompts to populate the KV/cache and materialize lazy buffers. Use the same corpus every run.
- Synthetic cache fill: if the model supports KV caching, replay N short sequences with typical user prefixes that exercise attention and kv paths. N tuned per-model (e.g., 50–200 prompts).
- Memory allocation priming: send a few long sequences to force peak memory allocations and placement decisions (helpful when allocation strategy depends on observed max-seq).
- No-priming baseline: occasionally run without priming to measure the magnitude of priming impact (useful for regression signals).

Measurement windows and metrics to export: (all exporters in JSON + CSV)
- Per-second tokens_out and tokens_in
- P50/P95/P99 latency (generation-only and end-to-end request)
- GPU util %, GPU memory used (peak+avg), GPU SM clock, PCIe/NVLink BW
- CPU sys/user, host memory pressure, swap use
- Batch sizes observed (server-side) and queue depth over time
- Number of dropped or retried requests

Repeatability checklist (pre-run):
- [ ] node warmed to baseline temperature (avoid fresh-VM cold start).
- [ ] same driver/container image, same CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN versions (recorded in artifact).
- [ ] background batch jobs disabled (no cron/monitor tasks).
- [ ] network path stable (run within same AZ, disable cross-AZ fallback).
- [ ] set OMP_NUM_THREADS and pin processes to core ranges.
- [ ] set affinity for loadgen workers and runtime threads.

Data capture and post-processing:
- Capture GPU traces (nsight-like or perf counters) for the warmup window and a representative 30s slice in steady-state.
- Persist raw logs: per-request start/end/latency/tokens into gzipped ndjson. Keep file names with seeds and run ids.
- Post-process script (tools/bench_post.py) produces: run-summary.json (flat fields), per-second CSV, and plots.
- Always save raw artifacts in run artifact bucket path: s3://redwood-bench/<commit>/<run-id>/

How we detect and report warmup drift:
1) For each run compute tokens/sec time series.
2) Smooth with moving median window (5s) and compute mean within measurement window.
3) Compare mean vs final 2 minutes window; if >3% delta classify as drift.
4) If any run in an N-run cohort shows drift, flag run and attach GPU traces for investigation.

Known pitfall cases and mitigations: 
- Case: first 30s low throughput due to lazy JIT/kernels. Mitigation: extend priming to include representative long seqs or force compilation path with a warmup compile step.
- Case: huge variance when sequence shapes vary. Mitigation: enforce bucketed/pinned shapes or pre-batching by token length.
- Case: RNG sampling drift (synthetic prompt generator). Mitigation: store and reuse pre-generated corpus.
- Case: caching across runs on multi-tenant node. Mitigation: run on isolated node or perform aggressive cache-clearing between runs (docker rebuild or node reboot).

Quick troubleshooting playbook if run fails repeatability gate:
- Check seed + artifact hash: identical inputs?
- Compare first-5-min traces: memory alloc patterns and cuBLAS kernel launches (use trace grep).
- Confirm runtime flags: env vars that change behavior (e.g., FAST_MATH, QUANTIZE_PATH).
- Re-run with single-worker single-GPU to isolate distributed scheduler noise.

Automation notes / engineering TODOs:
- tools/loadgen should support a --priming-corpus-file and enforce deterministic replay. (PR open GH #548)
- Add run-level metadata capture inside runtime (env + driver args) to ease triage.
- Implement an optional deterministic "compile-only" pass that warms kernel caches without producing network-visible traffic.

Open questions / experiments to try: 
- How much of drift is thermal vs JIT? Run cold vs warmed node with forced compilation to separate.
- Can a short sequence of synthetic micro-batches produce the same memory placement outcome as a long sequence? Measure using traced allocation timestamps.
- For models with multiple kernel variants: can we force a variant selection earlier in the run deterministically?

Notes to self / scraps:
- When writing artifacts, include cuda/cudnn versions and nvidia-smi -q output.
- Save a histogram of sequence lengths in every run.
- We should standardize "steady-state" definition across all benches (currently some teams use last 5m, some last 10m). Recommend last 10m for long runs, last 3m acceptable for quick CI.

References and prior experiments:
- GH PR #420: warmup priming experiments (contains raw plots)
- Confluence: runbook for throughput harness (older draft)
- JIRA INF-1998: kernel selection jitter investigation

Next steps (short):
- Lock a canonical priming corpus and add to tools/assets (Priya + Ethan) by 2024-12-15.
- Update loadgen to expose --priming-corpus-file and deterministic replay (Samir) by 2024-12-20.
- Run 10-cohort repeatability suite across 3 node types and collect summary by 2025-01-05.

If you copy anything from this: double-check seeds and corpus versions. This is intentionally prescriptive to reduce variance in our benchmarks, but we should keep occasional "no-priming" runs to ensure real-user behaviour signals are not being masked.

-- Priya
